title: Duke Energy and North Carolina regulators advance all-of-the-above plan to power the Carolinas’ growth while working to keep bills in check
summary: Duke Energy issued the following statement on yesterday’s order by the North Carolina Utilities Commission (NCUC) on the 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan, which charts how the company will meet rapid growth in the Carolinas while keeping affordability in focus.
body_markdown:
-


### **Order moves forward a balanced mix of natural gas, solar, batteries and nuclear development to keep the lights on – with customer costs front and center**


CHARLOTTE, N.C. – Duke Energy issued the following statement on[yesterday’s order](https://starw1.ncuc.gov/NCUC/PSC/PSCDocumentDetailsPageNCUC.aspx?DocumentId=6853bf2a-38f3-4c4a-83cc-76b122361de7&Class=Order) by the North Carolina Utilities Commission (NCUC) on the[2025 Carolinas Resource Plan](https://news.duke-energy.com/releases/duke-energy-files-2025-carolinas-resource-plan-continues-modernizing-energy-infrastructure-to-support-future-growth) , which charts how the company will meet rapid growth in the Carolinas while keeping affordability in focus.


**Our view:** “We know families and businesses are watching their energy bills closely, and we take that seriously,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy’s North Carolina president. “The plan reflects an all-of-the-above approach – natural gas, solar, batteries and new nuclear – shaped by our customers and many partners across the state. We appreciate the commission’s careful review, and we’re committed to working together to keep the lights on, support economic development and hold down costs as the Carolinas grow.”


**Meeting growth, together:** North Carolina is growing rapidly – that growth brings real opportunity and real questions about cost that no single energy source can address. That’s why the plan relies on an all-of-the-above approach: reliable natural gas, solar and battery storage, and continued work toward new nuclear power, backed by the energy efficiency and demand response programs customers already use to save money.


The plan was shaped through an open process that included input from the North Carolina Public Staff, customers, community and business leaders, and other stakeholders. Duke Energy will keep working with them – and with state leaders – on a path that protects reliability, supports jobs and makes sure the costs of growth are shared fairly, including ensuring that large new energy users help pay for the infrastructure they need.


The order moves the following new energy infrastructure forward – some of which is already under construction, while other projects will require additional project-specific review and approval, with continued opportunity for public input, before moving forward.


**Near-term Resources:**


- ***Solar:*** 2,300 megawatts (MW) of new solar generation, beyond the NCUC’s 2022 and 2024 resource plan orders – 8,100 MW total by 2034.
- ***Batteries:*** 2,700 MW of new battery energy storage beyond the NCUC’s 2022/24 orders – 5,400 MW total by 2034.
- ***Combined Cycles (CCs):*** 2,720 MW of additional capacity (CC4, CC5) beyond the 3,920 MW (CC1-3) in the NCUC’s 2022/24 orders – five CCs total by 2033.
- ***Combustion Turbines (CTs):*** 1,111 MW of additional CTs (CT5-7) beyond the 1,700 MW (CT1-4) in the NCUC’s 2022/24 orders – seven CTs total by 2032.


**Nuclear:**


- Approved continued development work supporting either small modular reactors or large light water reactor generation; authorized the company to develop and submit amendments to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for two AP1000 units at the W.S. Lee site in Cherokee County, S.C., and revisions to the combined license application for two AP1000 units at the Shearon Harris site in Wake County, N.C.
- Opened a new nuclear docket to provide quarterly updates on nuclear development progress and inform the NCUC’s evaluation of reactor technology, costs, financing, execution risks and customer protections before any decision to build a new nuclear plant.


**Why it matters:** North Carolina and South Carolina are two of the fastest-growing states in the nation, adding new neighbors, new businesses and new demand for power. To serve that growth, replace aging infrastructure and keep the system reliable, Duke Energy is investing in a balanced mix of resources across its dual-state system – and sharing the progress along the way – for the 4.8 million Carolinas customers who depend on it every day.


**Keeping costs in focus:** Every dollar matters to families and small businesses. The[2025 Carolinas Resource Plan](https://www.duke-energy.com/-/media/pdfs/our-company/irp-carolinas/2025-carolinas-resource-plan-fact-sheet.pdf) adapted to policy changes at the state and federal levels, and as a result, the plan’s projected cost to customers over the next decade was reduced by nearly half compared to the plan approved by regulators in 2024. Duke Energy is also pursuing additional ways to help hold down future costs in the Carolinas:


- ***Combining Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress:*** Effective Jan. 1, the combination is projected to save customers $2.3 billion from 2027 to 2040.
- ***Nuclear and Solar Tax Credits for Carolinas:*** Estimated $2.7 billion in net tax credits, including nuclear and solar production tax credits and investment tax credits, expected to be generated between 2025 and 2028 in the Carolinas.
- ***DOE Grants:*** U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) grant funding totaling more than $110 million to support reliability through transmission upgrades and power plant refurbishments in the Carolinas.
- ***DOE Loans:*** The company has applied for loans from the U.S. Department of Energy that represent potentially billions of dollars in additional customer savings.


What’s next: Construction is already underway at facilities like the[Person County Energy Complex](https://www.duke-energy.com/info/person) and the second battery storage facility replacing the retired Allen Plant, and will begin in 2027 at the approved[Anderson Natural Gas Project](https://www.duke-energy.com/info/anderson-natural-gas-plant-project) . Over the last year, the company completed three solar projects in the Carolinas totaling 151 MW, with construction about to begin on three more totaling 192 MW.[Regulators today also approved](https://starw1.ncuc.gov/NCUC/ViewFile.aspx?Id=eab93dc4-9b12-4333-b2dc-ae795efb4cec) the[planned combustion turbines](https://www.duke-energy.com/info/buck) where the former Buck coal plant once stood.


**A path forward together:** Duke Energy will continue to work with the Public Staff, state and local leaders, customers, and community and business partners as these projects move ahead – listening, sharing progress and adjusting as needs change. The company will also keep helping customers manage their bills through energy efficiency programs and payment assistance.


### **Duke Energy Carolinas**


Duke Energy Carolinas, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 20,800 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 3 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 24,000-square-mile service area in North Carolina and South Carolina.


### **Duke Energy Progress**


Duke Energy Progress, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 13,800 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 1.8 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 28,000-square-mile service area in North Carolina and South Carolina.


### **Duke Energy**


Duke Energy (NYSE: DUK), a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., is one of America’s largest energy holding companies. The company’s electric utilities serve 8.7 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, and collectively own 55,700 megawatts of energy capacity. Its natural gas utilities serve 1.6 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky.


Duke Energy is executing an energy modernization strategy, keeping customer value at the forefront as it invests in electric grid upgrades and efficient generation resources to strengthen the system and serve growing energy needs.
